Skin Lesion Classification (HAM10000): how much of the score is real?¶

The question: can a network tell seven kinds of skin lesion apart from a photo, including the dangerous one, melanoma? The legacy notebook reported 75% accuracy. That number is not trustworthy, and the reasons are the lesson: it balanced the classes by copying photos before splitting into train and test, so the test set was full of photos the network had already seen. How much does that inflate the score, what is the honest number, does a pretrained network help, does resolution matter, and what does the network actually do about melanoma?

How this notebook works. Each section starts with a plain-English explanation, then the code, then a "how to read this" note.

  1. The analogy
  2. Setup
  3. Audit the data
  4. Hypotheses and why we chose each test
  5. H1: do the patients behind each diagnosis differ?
  6. The models
  7. Splitting by lesion
  8. H2: how much does the legacy split inflate the score?
  9. H3: pretrained network, small network, and resolution
  10. H4: melanoma, and where the network gets confused
  11. Takeaways
  12. Limitations

Run it: uv run jupyter lab DL/skin-cancer-lesion-classification/ham10000.ipynb, or Run All in any Jupyter. The images (about 2.8 GB from the Harvard Dataverse, licence CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial use only) download themselves on the first run. It uses a GPU if present and takes about 45 minutes on one.

This is a teaching example, not a diagnostic tool.

1. 💡 The simple analogy¶

Imagine a student preparing for an exam with a practice test.

  • If the exam contains the same questions as the practice test, a high score proves only that the student memorised the answers. This is what the legacy notebook did: it photocopied the rare lesion photos to even out the classes, and only then split the photos into "practice" and "exam", so many exam photos were copies of practice photos.
  • Even without copies, one lesion was often photographed several times. An exam made of the same lesion from a slightly different angle is still not a fair test of recognising a lesion the student has never met.
  • An honest exam uses lesions the student has never seen.
  • Pretraining is a student who has already studied a million everyday photos: they know what edges and textures look like before they see a single lesion.
  • Balanced accuracy is the fair grade when most patients have harmless moles: it averages the score on each kind of lesion, so ignoring the rare ones cannot hide.

2. Setup¶

What: imports and named constants. Why: one place for numbers like the seed, the image size and the training budget keeps the notebook reproducible and avoids "magic numbers". With the seeds fixed (and the GPU set to deterministic mode), every model comes out the same each time you run it.

def fmt_p(p: float) -> str:
    """Formats a p-value, showing values below floating-point precision honestly.

    Args:
        p: The p-value.

    Returns:
        A short string such as ``3.2e-08`` or ``< 1e-300``.
    """
    return "< 1e-300" if p < 1e-300 else f"{p:.1e}"

3. Audit the data first¶

What: load the HAM10000 table (one row per photo: diagnosis, how the diagnosis was confirmed, patient age and sex, body site, and a lesion ID) and the 10,015 photos, cropped to the central square and shrunk to 128 x 128 pixels. Why: before training we should know how unbalanced the classes are, how many photos share a lesion, and whether the table already hints at the answer.

Problems in the legacy notebook this replaces: it resampled every class to 500 photos with replacement and only then split into train and test, so copies of the same photo sit on both sides; it ignored that many lesions have several photos; it shrank images to 32 x 32 pixels; it used the test set as validation data for 100 epochs; it reported accuracy on a class-balanced resample, which says nothing about real patients; it read images from Colab/Windows paths and relied on Keras APIs that no longer exist. It also saved a processed CSV that depended on those flaws.

In [2]:
def load_ham() -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]:
    """Downloads HAM10000 (once, into ``data/``) and returns its table and cached image pixels.

    Each photo is cropped to its central square and resized to ``CACHE_SIZE`` pixels, then cached
    in ``data/ham_{CACHE_SIZE}.npz`` so later runs start in seconds.

    Returns:
        The metadata table (one row per image) and a uint8 array of shape (n, S, S, 3) in the
        same row order.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the metadata does not have the expected shape.
    """
    for name, file_id in FILES.items():
        if not (DATA_DIR / name).exists():
            request = urllib.request.Request(  # the server refuses Python's default user agent
                f"{BASE_URL}/{file_id}?format=original", headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"}
            )
            with urllib.request.urlopen(request) as response, open(DATA_DIR / name, "wb") as out:
                shutil.copyfileobj(response, out)
    images_dir = DATA_DIR / "images"
    if not any(images_dir.glob("*.jpg")):
        for part in ("HAM10000_images_part_1.zip", "HAM10000_images_part_2.zip"):
            with zipfile.ZipFile(DATA_DIR / part) as zf:
                zf.extractall(images_dir)
    table = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "HAM10000_metadata.csv")
    if table.shape != (10_015, 8) or set(table["dx"]) != set(CLASSES):
        raise ValueError("Unexpected HAM10000 metadata")
    cache = DATA_DIR / f"ham_{CACHE_SIZE}.npz"
    if cache.exists():
        return table, np.load(cache)["pixels"]

    def read(image_id: str) -> np.ndarray:
        with Image.open(images_dir / f"{image_id}.jpg") as im:
            side = min(im.size)
            left, top = (im.width - side) // 2, (im.height - side) // 2
            square = im.convert("RGB").crop((left, top, left + side, top + side))
            return np.asarray(square.resize((CACHE_SIZE, CACHE_SIZE), Image.BILINEAR))

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as pool:
        pixels = np.stack(list(pool.map(read, table["image_id"])))
    np.savez(cache, pixels=pixels)
    return table, pixels

How to read this:

  • 10,015 photos of 7,470 lesions. 1,956 lesions were photographed more than once, up to 6 times. Any split that works photo by photo will put the same lesion on both sides.
  • The classes are very unbalanced: naevi (harmless moles, nv) are 6,705 photos, melanoma 1,113, benign keratosis 1,099, basal cell carcinoma 514, actinic keratosis 327, vascular 142 and dermatofibroma 115. Always guessing "nv" scores 66.9% accuracy, while guessing among the seven classes scores 14.3% balanced accuracy.
  • 57 photos have no age and 57 have an unknown sex.
  • How a diagnosis was confirmed depends on the class: every melanoma, basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratosis was confirmed by biopsy (histo, 100%), while 55% of the naevi were confirmed only by follow-up and 8% by consensus. The table's own "how was it confirmed" column therefore leaks information about the class, so we must not use it as a feature.

4. Hypotheses and why we chose each test¶

# Question H₀ (nothing interesting) Hₐ Test
H1 Do patients differ by diagnosis (age, sex, body site)? Same distribution Differs Kruskal-Wallis with ε²; chi-square with Cramér's V
H2 Does "resample, then split" inflate the score? Same balanced accuracy under all splits Legacy split is higher 5 seeds per split design, Mann-Whitney U; share of test photos also in training
H3 Does a pretrained network beat a small one, and does resolution matter? Same balanced accuracy Differs 3 to 5 seeds, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis; a metadata-only baseline
H4 How well does it find melanoma? n/a (estimation) n/a Per-class recall with Wilson CIs, melanoma ROC and sensitivity at fixed specificity

Why these tests? Ages and scores are not normally distributed, so rank-based tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney) are safer than t-tests. With 10,015 photos nearly everything is statistically significant, so we report effect sizes (ε², Cramér's V). Balanced accuracy (the mean of the recall of each class) replaces plain accuracy because of the class imbalance.

5. H1: do the patients behind each diagnosis differ?¶

What: we test whether the age of the patient differs between diagnoses (Kruskal-Wallis, with ε² as the effect size), and whether sex, body site and how the diagnosis was confirmed are associated with the diagnosis (chi-square, with Cramér's V). Why: if age and body site already say a lot about the diagnosis, a model could lean on them rather than on the lesion; and if the confirmation type does, it is a shortcut to avoid.

    ", ".join(f"{c} {np.median(g):.0f}" for c, g in zip(CLASSES, groups, strict=True)),
)


def cramers_v(table: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Chi-square test of independence with Cramer's V as the effect size.

    Args:
        table: Contingency table of counts.

    Returns:
        The chi-square statistic, its p-value and Cramer's V.
    """
    chi2, p, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
    n = table.to_numpy().sum()
    return chi2, p, float(np.sqrt(chi2 / (n * (min(table.shape) - 1))))


for column in ["sex", "localization", "dx_type"]:
    chi2, p, v = cramers_v(pd.crosstab(meta["dx"], meta[column]))
    print(f"Diagnosis vs {column}: chi-square = {chi2:.0f}, p = {fmt_p(p)}, Cramer's V = {v:.2f}")

How to read this:

  • Age differs a lot between diagnoses: Kruskal-Wallis H = 2,271, p < 1e-300, ε² = 0.228 (a large effect). Median ages: naevi 45, dermatofibroma 50, vascular 55, melanoma 60, benign keratosis 65, actinic keratosis and basal cell carcinoma 70. We reject H₀.
  • Body site matters too: Cramér's V = 0.22. Sex is a weak factor (V = 0.07, though the p-value of 2.4e-17 is tiny with this many photos).
  • The confirmation type is the strongest association (V = 0.39) and is a shortcut we exclude from every model.
  • Patient age, sex and body site alone carry real signal about the diagnosis, which we measure in H3 with a model that never sees a photo.

6. The models¶

What: the networks and helper functions we use throughout.

  • A small CNN: three convolution blocks with batch norm and global pooling, in the spirit of the legacy notebook.
  • ResNet-18 pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned.
  • Training: flip and transpose augmentation (lesions have no up or down), AdamW with a one-cycle learning rate, a loss weighted by the inverse frequency of each class, a fixed number of epochs, and the final epoch is what is scored: the test photos never choose anything.
  • The score: balanced accuracy, the mean per-class recall. A network that always says "naevus" gets 14.3%.
In [5]:
def to_size(images: np.ndarray, size: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Resizes cached images to ``size`` pixels and puts them on the compute device (uint8).

    Args:
        images: uint8 array of shape (n, S, S, 3).
        size: Target side length in pixels.

    Returns:
        A uint8 tensor of shape (n, size, size, 3).
    """
    out = []
    for start in range(0, len(images), 1000):
        chunk = torch.tensor(images[start : start + 1000], device=DEVICE)
        chunk = chunk.permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float()
        if size != chunk.shape[-1]:
            chunk = F.interpolate(chunk, size=(size, size), mode="area")
        out.append(chunk.round().clamp(0, 255).byte().permute(0, 2, 3, 1))
    return torch.cat(out)


def to_input(batch: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Turns uint8 images (batch, H, W, 3) into normalised float tensors (batch, 3, H, W)."""
    x = batch.permute(0, 3, 1, 2).float().div(255)
    return (x - IMAGENET_MEAN.to(x.device)) / IMAGENET_STD.to(x.device)


def augment(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Random flips and a random transpose per image (skin lesions have no fixed orientation).

    Args:
        x: Batch of images, shape (batch, 3, H, W).

    Returns:
        The augmented batch.
    """
    n = len(x)
    flip_h = torch.rand(n, device=x.device) < 0.5
    flip_v = torch.rand(n, device=x.device) < 0.5
    swap = torch.rand(n, device=x.device) < 0.5
    x = torch.where(flip_h[:, None, None, None], x.flip(3), x)
    x = torch.where(flip_v[:, None, None, None], x.flip(2), x)
    return torch.where(swap[:, None, None, None], x.transpose(2, 3), x)


class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    """Three convolution blocks (like the legacy notebook, with batch norm) and global pooling."""

    def __init__(self, n_classes: int = 7) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        blocks, width = [], 3
        for out in (64, 128, 256):
            blocks += [
                nn.Conv2d(width, out, 3, padding=1),
                nn.BatchNorm2d(out),
                nn.ReLU(),
                nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            ]
            width = out
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            *blocks, nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Dropout(0.3)
        )
        self.head = nn.Linear(width, n_classes)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Class scores for a batch of images."""
        return self.head(self.features(x))


def make_resnet(n_classes: int = 7) -> nn.Module:
    """ResNet-18 pretrained on ImageNet, with a new head for the seven diagnoses."""
    weights = torchvision.models.ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1
    net = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights=weights)
    net.fc = nn.Linear(net.fc.in_features, n_classes)
    return net


def train_classifier(
    kind: str,
    images: torch.Tensor,
    train_idx: np.ndarray,
    seed: int,
    class_weighted: bool = True,
    epochs: int | None = None,
) -> nn.Module:
    """Trains a lesion classifier for a fixed number of epochs (test photos are never used).

    Args:
        kind: ``"small"`` or ``"resnet"``.
        images: uint8 images at the training size, shape (n, H, W, 3).
        train_idx: Indices (into ``images``; repeats allowed) to train on.
        seed: Seed for weights and batch order.
        class_weighted: Weight the loss by inverse class frequency in ``train_idx``.
        epochs: Override the default number of epochs.

    Returns:
        The trained network in evaluation mode.
    """
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = (SmallCNN() if kind == "small" else make_resnet()).to(DEVICE)
    n_epochs = epochs or (EPOCHS_SMALL if kind == "small" else EPOCHS_RESNET)
    lr = 2e-3 if kind == "small" else 3e-4
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=1e-4)
    steps = n_epochs * int(np.ceil(len(train_idx) / BATCH))
    scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(optimizer, max_lr=lr, total_steps=steps)
    train_labels = torch.tensor(y[train_idx], device=DEVICE)
    weight = None
    if class_weighted:
        freq = torch.bincount(train_labels, minlength=7).float().clamp(min=1)
        weight = (len(train_labels) / (7 * freq)).to(DEVICE)
    index = torch.tensor(train_idx, device=DEVICE)
    for _ in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        order = torch.randperm(len(index), device=DEVICE)
        for start in range(0, len(index), BATCH):
            pick = order[start : start + BATCH]
            batch = augment(to_input(images[index[pick]]))
            loss = F.cross_entropy(model(batch), train_labels[pick], weight=weight)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
            scheduler.step()
    return model.eval()


def predict_scores(model: nn.Module, images: torch.Tensor, idx: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Class probabilities for the given photos.

    Args:
        model: A trained classifier.
        images: uint8 images at the model's size.
        idx: Which photos to score.

    Returns:
        Probabilities of shape (len(idx), 7).
    """
    out = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for start in range(0, len(idx), 512):
            batch = images[torch.tensor(idx[start : start + 512], device=DEVICE)]
            out.append(F.softmax(model(to_input(batch)), dim=1).cpu().numpy())
    return np.concatenate(out)


def balanced_accuracy(truth: np.ndarray, pred: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Mean of the per-class recalls: 1/7 for guessing, 1 for perfect, whatever the class mix."""
    return float(np.mean([(pred[truth == k] == k).mean() for k in range(7) if (truth == k).any()]))

How to read this: these cells only define the models and helpers, so there is nothing to interpret yet. The results start in the next sections.

7. Splitting by lesion¶

What: the honest split. Whole lesions (all their photos together) are assigned to training (70%), validation (15%) or test (15%), separately for each diagnosis so that every set has every class. An assert stops the notebook if any lesion appears in two sets. Why: it is the only way to ask the question that matters: does the network recognise a lesion it has never seen?

In [6]:
def lesion_split(
    fractions: tuple[float, float, float], seed: int = SEED
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Splits photos into train, validation and test sets so that no lesion crosses sets.

    Lesions are shuffled within each diagnosis, so every set keeps every class.

    Args:
        fractions: Shares of lesions for train, validation and test.
        seed: Seed for the shuffle.

    Returns:
        Index arrays of photos for the three sets.
    """
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    lesion_class = meta.groupby("lesion_id")["dx"].first()
    bucket = {}
    for cls in CLASSES:
        ids = lesion_class.index[lesion_class == cls].to_numpy()
        ids = gen.permutation(ids)
        cut1 = int(round(fractions[0] * len(ids)))
        cut2 = cut1 + int(round(fractions[1] * len(ids)))
        for i, lesion in enumerate(ids):
            bucket[lesion] = 0 if i < cut1 else (1 if i < cut2 else 2)
    which = np.array([bucket[lesion] for lesion in lesions])
    return tuple(np.flatnonzero(which == b) for b in range(3))


train_idx, val_idx, test_idx = lesion_split((0.70, 0.15, 0.15))
for name, idx in [("train", train_idx), ("validation", val_idx), ("test", test_idx)]:
    cls_counts = np.bincount(y[idx], minlength=7)
    print(
        f"{name:10s}: {len(idx):5,} photos from {len(set(lesions[idx])):5,} lesions; "
        + ", ".join(f"{c} {n}" for c, n in zip(CLASSES, cls_counts, strict=True))
    )
assert not set(lesions[train_idx]) & set(lesions[test_idx])
assert not set(lesions[train_idx]) & set(lesions[val_idx])

train     : 6,984 photos from 5,230 lesions; akiec 231, bcc 360, bkl 761, df 79, mel 782, nv 4672, vasc 99
validation: 1,541 photos from 1,120 lesions; akiec 50, bcc 80, bkl 175, df 16, mel 174, nv 1021, vasc 25

How to read this:

  • Training: 6,984 photos from 5,230 lesions. Validation: 1,541 photos from 1,120 lesions. Test: 1,490 photos from 1,120 lesions, with no lesion shared.
  • The test set holds 1,012 naevi, 157 melanomas, 163 benign keratoses, 74 basal cell carcinomas, 46 actinic keratoses, 20 dermatofibromas and 18 vascular lesions. The smallest classes have so few test photos that their per-class results will be uncertain (see H4).

8. H2: how much does the legacy split inflate the score?¶

What: we reproduce the legacy recipe and compare it with two cleaner ones, all with the same small network at 32 x 32 pixels, trained 5 times each, and all scored by balanced accuracy on a held-out test set:

  1. Legacy: resample every class to 500 photos with replacement, then split 75/25 at random.
  2. Split photos, then resample: split the 10,015 photos at random, then resample only the training part to 500 per class.
  3. Split lesions, then resample: split whole lesions, then resample only the training part.

We also count how many test photos have an identical photo in training, and how many belong to a lesion that is in training.

In [7]:
def resample_to(idx: np.ndarray, per_class: int, seed: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Draws ``per_class`` photos of every diagnosis with replacement, as the legacy notebook did.

    Args:
        idx: Photos to draw from.
        per_class: Photos per class after resampling.
        seed: Seed for the draw.

    Returns:
        Indices (with repeats) of the resampled photos.
    """
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return np.concatenate([gen.choice(idx[y[idx] == k], per_class, replace=True) for k in range(7)])


def protocol_split(protocol: str, seed: int = 42) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Train and test indices for the three ways of splitting that this notebook compares.

    Args:
        protocol: ``"legacy"`` resamples every class to ``PER_CLASS`` photos and then splits the
            result at random; ``"image"`` splits photos at random and resamples the training part
            only; ``"lesion"`` splits whole lesions and resamples the training part only.
        seed: Seed for the splits.

    Returns:
        Training indices (with repeats) and test indices.
    """
    gen = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if protocol == "legacy":
        pool = resample_to(np.arange(len(meta)), PER_CLASS, seed)
        order = gen.permutation(len(pool))
        cut = int(0.75 * len(pool))
        return pool[order[:cut]], pool[order[cut:]]
    if protocol == "image":
        order = gen.permutation(len(meta))
        cut = int(0.75 * len(meta))
        return resample_to(order[:cut], PER_CLASS, seed), order[cut:]
    tr, _, te = lesion_split((0.75, 0.0, 0.25), seed)
    return resample_to(tr, PER_CLASS, seed), te


leak_info = {}
for protocol in ("legacy", "image", "lesion"):
    tr, te = protocol_split(protocol)
    same_photo = np.isin(meta["image_id"].to_numpy()[te], meta["image_id"].to_numpy()[tr]).mean()
    same_lesion = np.isin(lesions[te], lesions[tr]).mean()
    leak_info[protocol] = (same_photo, same_lesion, len(set(tr)), len(te))
    print(
        f"{protocol:7s}: {len(tr):,} training draws ({len(set(tr)):,} distinct photos), "
        f"{len(te):,} test photos; test photos whose identical photo is in training: "
        f"{same_photo:.1%}; whose lesion is in training: {same_lesion:.1%}"
    )

image  : 3,500 training draws (1,914 distinct photos), 2,504 test photos; test photos whose identical photo is in training: 0.0%; whose lesion is in training: 14.6%

How to read this:


    

  • The legacy split is full of leaks: 53.6% of its test photos have an identical copy in the training set, and 65.1% belong to a lesion that is in training. Splitting photos first removes the exact copies (0%) but still leaves 14.6% of the test photos from lesions seen in training. Only the lesion split has none (0%).
    • 

  • The score falls with every fix: balanced accuracy 73.6% (legacy), 67.5% (photos split first) and 63.2% (lesions split) with standard deviations of 0.5 to 1.2 points. The legacy number is +6.1 points above the photo split and +10.4 points above the lesion split, higher in all 5 of 5 runs (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0079, the smallest value 5 against 5 runs can give). We reject H₀.
    • 

  • The legacy notebook's reported 75% accuracy is almost exactly what this recipe produces (73.8%), so it measured how well the network remembered photos, not how well it recognises lesions.
    • 

  • Under the honest split, the same network scores 63.2% (plain accuracy 64.2%): much better than guessing (14.3%), far worse than the headline.
    • 























9. H3: pretrained network, small network, and resolution¶
What: on the honest lesion split (70/15/15) we train the small CNN at 64 pixels (5 seeds) and the pretrained ResNet-18 at 32, 64 and 128 pixels (3 seeds each), with class-weighted training, and score balanced accuracy, plain accuracy and the macro one-vs-rest AUC on the test lesions. Two reference points: always guessing the most common class, and a metadata-only model (gradient boosting on age, sex and body site) that never sees a photo. Why: it separates what the photos add from what the patient's age and body site already tell us.


















In [10]:






def macro_scores(truth: np.ndarray, probs: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Balanced accuracy, plain accuracy and macro one-vs-rest AUC.

    Args:
        truth: True class indices.
        probs: Predicted class probabilities.

    Returns:
        A dict with ``balanced``, ``accuracy`` and ``auc``.
    """
    pred = probs.argmax(1)
    return {
        "balanced": balanced_accuracy(truth, pred),
        "accuracy": float((pred == truth).mean()),
        "auc": roc_auc_score(
            truth, probs, multi_class="ovr", average="macro", labels=list(range(7))
        ),
    }


resample_train = resample_to(train_idx, PER_CLASS * 2, SEED)  # balanced training draws
runs = []
test_probs = {}
val_probs = {}
for kind, size, n_runs in [
    ("small", 64, N_SEEDS),
    ("resnet", 32, N_SEEDS_RESNET),
    ("resnet", 64, N_SEEDS_RESNET),
    ("resnet", 128, N_SEEDS_RESNET),
]:
    images = to_size(PIXELS, size)
    for seed in range(n_runs):
        model = train_classifier(kind, images, train_idx, seed, class_weighted=True)
        probs = predict_scores(model, images, test_idx)
        test_probs[(kind, size, seed)] = probs
        if seed == 0:
            val_probs[(kind, size)] = predict_scores(model, images, val_idx)
        runs.append({"model": kind, "size": size, "seed": seed, **macro_scores(y[test_idx], probs)})
runs = pd.DataFrame(runs)

base_rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
meta_cols = pd.get_dummies(
    meta[["age", "sex", "localization"]], columns=["sex", "localization"], dtype=float
).fillna(meta["age"].median())
meta_model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED, class_weight="balanced").fit(
    meta_cols.iloc[train_idx], y[train_idx]
)
meta_probs = meta_model.predict_proba(meta_cols.iloc[test_idx])
meta_scores = macro_scores(y[test_idx], meta_probs)
summary = runs.groupby(["model", "size"]).agg(
    runs=("seed", "size"),
    balanced=("balanced", "mean"),
    balanced_sd=("balanced", "std"),
    accuracy=("accuracy", "mean"),
    auc=("auc", "mean"),
)
print(f"Test set: {len(test_idx):,} photos from lesions never seen in training")
print(
    f"Always guessing 'nv': accuracy {(y[test_idx] == 5).mean():.1%}, "
    f"balanced accuracy {100 / 7:.1f}%"
)
print(

    f"{meta_scores['balanced']:.1%}, accuracy {meta_scores['accuracy']:.1%}, "

)
print(
    (summary * 100).round(1).assign(runs=summary["runs"], auc=summary["auc"].round(3)).to_string()
)

How to read this:


    

  • The metadata alone beats guessing by a long way: age, sex and body site give 35.0% balanced accuracy (AUC 0.768), against 14.3% for guessing. A good share of what a photo-based model "knows" can come from the kind of patient, not the lesion.
    • 

  • A pretrained network is much better than a small one: at 64 pixels ResNet-18 reaches 65.4% (sd 0.5) against 55.2% (sd 1.0) for the small CNN, a gain of 10.2 points (Mann-Whitney p = 0.036, the smallest value 3 against 5 runs can give). We reject H₀.
    • 

  • Resolution matters: ResNet-18 scores 57.6% at 32 pixels, 65.4% at 64 and 68.7% at 128 (sd 2.0); Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.027. The legacy 32-pixel images throw away much of what the photo can show.
    • 

  • The best model (ResNet-18, 128 pixels, seed 0) reaches 71.0% balanced accuracy (95% bootstrap CI 65.9% to 75.8%), and its plain accuracy averages 76.3% (the AUC is 0.936). Plain accuracy is higher than balanced because the test set is two-thirds naevi.
    • 

  • So the honest picture: about 69% balanced accuracy for a pretrained network at 128 pixels (against the legacy 75% accuracy on leaked data), with resolution and pretraining the two things that clearly move it.
    • 























10. H4: melanoma, and where the network gets confused¶
What: for the seed-0 ResNet at 128 pixels, a confusion matrix and the recall of each class with 95% Wilson intervals. Then melanoma against everything else: the AUC, and the share of melanomas caught at thresholds set on the validation lesions to keep 80%, 90% or 95% of the other lesions unflagged (the "specificity"). Why: melanoma is the dangerous lesion, and missing one is much worse than a needless biopsy, so the threshold is a clinical decision, not just a statistical one.


















In [13]:






confusion = np.zeros((7, 7), dtype=int)
for t, p in zip(truth, pred128, strict=True):
    confusion[t, p] += 1
recall_rows = []
for k, c in enumerate(CLASSES):
    n, hit = confusion[k].sum(), confusion[k, k]
    low, high = proportion_confint(hit, n, method="wilson")
    recall_rows.append(
        {
            "class": c,
            "photos": n,
            "recall": hit / n,
            "ci_low": low,
            "ci_high": high,
            "most common mistake": CLASSES[
                np.argsort(-np.where(np.arange(7) == k, -1, confusion[k]))[0]
            ],
        }
    )
recall_table = pd.DataFrame(recall_rows).set_index("class")
print(recall_table.round(3).to_string())
off = confusion.copy()
np.fill_diagonal(off, 0)
top = np.dstack(np.unravel_index(np.argsort(-off, axis=None)[:4], off.shape))[0]
print("\nFour most common mix-ups (true -> predicted: photos):")
for t, p in top:
    print(f"  {CLASSES[t]} -> {CLASSES[p]}: {off[t, p]}")
mel = CLASSES.index("mel")
y_mel = (truth == mel).astype(int)
mel_score = probs128[:, mel]
print(f"\nMelanoma vs everything else: AUC = {roc_auc_score(y_mel, mel_score):.3f}")
val_truth = y[val_idx]
val_neg = val_probs[("resnet", 128)][val_truth != mel][:, mel]
op_rows = []
for spec in (0.80, 0.90, 0.95):
    threshold = np.quantile(val_neg, spec)
    flagged = mel_score > threshold
    caught = int(flagged[y_mel == 1].sum())
    low, high = proportion_confint(caught, int(y_mel.sum()), method="wilson")
    op_rows.append(
        {
            "target specificity": spec,
            "melanomas caught": caught / y_mel.sum(),
            "ci_low": low,
            "ci_high": high,
            "actual specificity": 1 - flagged[y_mel == 0].mean(),
        }
    )
mel_ops = pd.DataFrame(op_rows).set_index("target specificity")
print(mel_ops.round(3).to_string())
print(f"Melanoma photos in the test set: {int(y_mel.sum())}")

How to read this:


    

  • Per-class recall (95% CI): vascular 88.9% (67.2% to 96.9%, only 18 photos), naevi 81.2% (78.7% to 83.5%), basal cell carcinoma 78.4% (67.7% to 86.2%), benign keratosis 68.1% (60.6% to 74.8%), melanoma 67.5% (59.8% to 74.3%), actinic keratosis 63.0% (48.6% to 75.5%) and dermatofibroma 50.0% (29.9% to 70.1%, only 20 photos). The small classes have very wide intervals, so their rankings are unreliable.
    • 

  • The biggest confusion is between naevi and melanoma: 104 naevi are called melanoma and 26 melanomas are called naevi; the next most common mix-ups are naevi called benign keratosis (57) and benign keratosis called melanoma (23). These are the look-alike pairs a dermatologist also finds hard.
    • 

  • Melanoma against all other lesions has an AUC of 0.900. With the threshold set for 80% specificity (79.2% on the test) the network catches 85.4% of melanomas (CI 79.0% to 90.0%); for 90% specificity (89.0%), 66.9% (59.2% to 73.8%); for 95% specificity (93.8%), 56.1% (48.2% to 63.6%). Every step towards fewer false alarms costs a large share of the melanomas.
    • 

  • The threshold is a clinical choice: this network would miss between one in seven and nearly one in two melanomas depending on the setting, which is why such a tool can only support a clinician, never replace one.
    • 























11. 🎯 Takeaways¶
    

  1. Never resample before splitting. In the legacy recipe 53.6% of test photos have an identical copy in training, and 65.1% share a lesion with training.
    2. 

  2. The honest score is much lower: with the same small network, balanced accuracy is 73.6% under the legacy split and 63.2% when whole lesions are held out (+10.4 points, 5 of 5 runs).
    3. 

  3. Use a metric that respects the imbalance: always guessing "nevus" is 66.9% accurate and 14.3% balanced accuracy.
    4. 

  4. Pretraining and resolution are what help: ResNet-18 beats the small CNN by 10.2 points at 64 pixels, and goes from 57.6% (32 px) to 68.7% (128 px).
    5. 

  5. Patient information is a strong signal on its own (35.0% balanced accuracy from age, sex and body site) and the "how confirmed" column is a shortcut to avoid.
    6. 

  6. Melanoma is found only at a price: AUC 0.900, but 85.4% caught at 79% specificity and 56.1% at 94%. The main confusion is naevus versus melanoma.
    7. 























12. ⚠️ Limitations¶
    

  • One dataset from two clinics (Austria and Australia), mostly fair-skinned patients and dermoscopic photos; the results will not carry over to other skin tones, cameras or phone photos.
    • 

  • Lesion IDs are the best available grouping, but the same patient can have several lesions, so a patient-level split would be stricter still.
    • 

  • Few seeds (5 and 3), so some p-values sit at their minimum possible value; and the small classes have very few test photos (18 and 20), so their recall intervals are wide.
    • 

  • Images are cropped to the central square and resized, and the training budget is short (30 epochs for the small CNN, 8 for ResNet); larger images and longer training would raise the scores.
    • 

  • The leakage experiment uses a 32-pixel small CNN (to mirror the legacy notebook), and its three test sets are different photos, so a point or so of difference could be noise; the 10-point gap is far larger.
    • 

  • Thresholds were set on one validation split; other splits would move them.
    •
